implementation_notes: The platform library provides the whole lock: pthread_rwlock_t with rdlock/wrlock/tryrdlock/trywrlock/unlock, initialised statically (PTHREAD_RWLOCK_INITIALIZER) or with pthread_rwlock_init, plus attributes for the priority policy (on glibc, PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_READER_NP is the default and PTHREAD_RWLOCK_PREFER_WRITER_NONRECURSIVE_NP makes writers win at the cost of recursive read locking) and PTHREAD_PROCESS_SHARED for shared-memory use. C11 <threads.h> ships only mtx_t and cnd_t, so portable C11 has no reader-writer type and must use pthreads or hand-build the gate. The classic structure is still justified over a plain mutex wherever reads dominate and a mutex would serialise them; in the write-heavy case a plain mutex is both simpler and faster.
pitfalls: Recursive read locking is allowed but every successful rdlock needs its own unlock; an unbalanced unlock leaves the lock permanently held.
A caller holding the write lock may deadlock on rdlock (EDEADLK where detected, otherwise undefined); upgrades are not supported, so unlock first.
On glibc the default policy is read-preferring, so a constant reader stream starves writers unless the writer-preferring (non-recursive) attribute is requested explicitly.
An uninitialised or already-destroyed rwlock is undefined behaviour; static initialisation or pthread_rwlock_init must precede any use, and destroy must come before the memory is reused.
